publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXV). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: CVIII. Porro ex dictis facile colligitur recentiorum Thomistarum doctrinam, quam exponit Didacus Alvarez, e diametro oppositam esse doctrinae quam tradit Molina, circa gratiam illam quae dicitur efficax, & cui tribuitur hominis conversio. Prorsus enim inter se pugnant, sive spectetur modus quo gratia hominem movet ad actus quibus ad Deum convertitur, sive natura ipsa & quidditas gratiae, & qua in re illa ponenda est.
english: Thesis CVIII. From all this it is easy to see that the doctrine of the recent Thomists, as Diego Alvarez presents it, stands diametrically opposed to Molina's teaching about the grace called efficacious, the grace to which a person's conversion is ascribed. The two are in complete conflict, whether we look at the way grace moves a person to the acts by which he turns to God, or at the nature and quiddity of grace itself and where it is to be located.

source_text: CIX. Nam quod attinet ad modum operandi gratiae, Thomistae recentiores, ut Didacus Alvarez, volunt gratiam illam per quam homo convertitur, esse efficacem per se, neque talem reddi per liberi arbitrii consensum, sed illa potenter & infallibiliter liberum arbitrium ad consensum determinari; sicut ante fuit expositum. Contra vero Molina, & qui eum sequuntur, pertendunt gratiam quae hominem convertit, ita libero arbitrio subjici, ut efficacia ejus a consensu liberi arbitrii pendeat, & sit in libera hominis potestate illam vel efficacem, vel inefficacem reddere, quorum utrumque de facto saepius eveniat.
english: Thesis CIX. On the way grace works, the recent Thomists, Alvarez among them, hold that the grace by which a person is converted is efficacious of itself. It is not made so by the consent of free choice; rather, as was explained earlier, it determines free choice to consent, powerfully and infallibly.

Molina and his followers maintain the opposite: the grace that converts a person is subject to free choice in such a way that its efficacy depends on free choice's consent. It lies in a person's free power to make it efficacious or inefficacious, and in fact each of these quite often happens.

source_text: CX. Quod spectat autem essentiam gratiae, qua movetur voluntas ad actus conversionis, & quae conversionem reipsa operatur, Recentiores Thomistae illam ponunt ut supra dictum, in motione aliqua virtuosa, quae habet esse quoddam incompletum, & est in voluntate per modum quo colores sunt in aere, & impetus in re quae impellitur. Molina vero gratiam quae, consentiente libero arbitrio, hominem efficaciter movet ad conversionem, ponit in affectibus quibusdam voluntatis, ex praevia mentis illuminatione ortis, quibus Deus per suum influxum se inserens, allicit voluntatem ut velit, & vires volendi tribuit, simulque concurrit cum voluntate si voluerit.
english: Thesis CX. As for the essence of the grace by which the will is moved to the acts of conversion and which actually brings conversion about, the recent Thomists, as was said above, place it in a virtual motion. This motion has an incomplete kind of being and is in the will as colours are in the air, or as impetus is in a thing that is being driven along.

Molina places the grace that moves a person efficaciously to conversion, when free choice consents, in certain affections of the will that arise from a prior illumination of the mind. God inserts himself into them by his influence, draws the will to will, gives it the strength to will, and concurs with the will at the same time, if it wills.

source_text: CXI. Proinde hac in parte propius a Molina Jansenius distat quam Thomistae recentiores. Quanquam enim cum illis Jansenius prorsus consentiat circa modum operandi gratiae efficacis, contendens efficaciam salutaris Christi gratiae nullatenus a consensu arbitrii humani pendere, sed consensum illum per se efficere, idque infallibiliter & insuperabiliter; nihilominus quod spectat naturam & substantiam gratiae quae dicitur efficax, minus abest ejus sententia a doctrina Molinae, quam a Doctrina Thomistarum. Quippe, ut ex antedictis manifestum est, gratiam illam efficacem, cui, juxta ipsum, hominis conversio, & omnia bona fidelium opera in solidum tribui debent, constituit in quibusdam affectibus amoris & desiderii, qui ab hominis voluntate, non libere quidem, sed active procedunt, ejusque sunt actus vitales, & quibus voluntas ad bonum libere amplectendum fertur & inducitur. Tales enim affectus intelligit nomine coelestis suavitatis & delectationis, in qua gratiam efficacem ponit.
english: Thesis CXI. On this point, then, Jansenius stands closer to Molina than the recent Thomists do. He agrees with the Thomists entirely on the way efficacious grace works, contending that the efficacy of Christ's saving grace in no way depends on the consent of human choice but produces that consent of itself, infallibly and insuperably. Yet on the nature and substance of the grace called efficacious, his view is less far from Molina's doctrine than from the Thomists'.

As is clear from what was said earlier, he places this efficacious grace, to which in his view a person's conversion and all the good works of the faithful must be wholly ascribed, in certain affections of love and desire. These proceed from the human will, not freely but actively; they are its vital acts, and by them the will is carried and led to embrace the good freely. Such are the affections he means by the name of heavenly sweetness and delight, in which he places efficacious grace.

source_text: CXII. Verum in eo differt a Molina, quod affectus istiusmodi, secundum Molinae doctrinam, mere naturaliter in voluntate oriuntur, posita mentis illuminatione: nec aliud praestat Deus, quam quod affectibus illis peculiari influxu se ingerit, eosque reddit supernaturales. Juxta Jansenium vero, posita quacunque mentis illuminatione, affectus isti in hominis corrupti voluntate per naturam non exurgunt, sed necesse est illos totos coelitus immitti, non simpliciter quadam divina motione acui, & intendi, ut fiant supernaturales.
english: Thesis CXII. He differs from Molina, however, in this. On Molina's doctrine such affections arise in the will purely by nature once the mind is illuminated, and God does no more than thrust himself into them by a special influence and make them supernatural.

On Jansenius's view, whatever illumination of the mind is given, these affections do not rise by nature in the will of fallen man. They must be sent into it wholly from heaven, and not merely sharpened and heightened by some divine motion so as to become supernatural.

source_text: CXIV. Praeterea Molina ad naturam voluntatis absolute consideratae pertinere existimat, ut statim atque intellectus aliquod objectum ipsi offert ut bonum & delectabile, erga illud motu quodam afficiatur, & tangatur affectu, qui voluntatem illicit & proritat, ut tale objectum libere amplectatur. Nec putat voluntatem in objectum aliquod ut bonum libere ferri, quin ejusmodi motus & affectus naturaliter exoriens in ea praecesserit. Adeoque quum homo, & Angelus integer, a vero bono declinare coepit, & terrenum ac privatum bonum spirituali & divino praeferre, in utroque malam voluntatem, juxta ipsum, antecessit ejusmodi motus & affectus, quo homo ad pomum vetitum comedendum, Angelus ad propriam excellentiam admirandam atque suspiciendam, excitabatur & alliciebatur.
english: Thesis CXIV. Molina further holds that it belongs to the nature of the will, considered absolutely, that as soon as the intellect presents it with some object as good and delightful, it is moved toward that object by a certain motion and touched by an affection. That affection entices and provokes the will to embrace such an object freely. He does not think the will is ever borne freely toward any object as good unless a motion and affection of this kind, arising naturally in it, has gone before.

So when man and the angel, still unfallen, began to turn away from the true good and to prefer an earthly, private good to the spiritual and divine, in each case, on his view, the evil will was preceded by such a motion and affection. By it the man was roused and drawn to eat the forbidden fruit, and the angel to admire and look up to his own excellence.

source_text: CXV. Jansenius autem illum amorem & desiderium, quod delectationis nomine significat, & quo voluntas jam trahitur, priusquam quicquam libere velit & amplectatur, ac quo praesertim illam affici necesse est, antequam prosequatur bonum coeleste & spirituale, necessario praecedere non censet omnes voluntatis actus, si consideretur absolute, & citra infirmitatem per peccatum contractam. Etenim secundum illius doctrinam, non est simpliciter de natura voluntatis, ut non valeat libere bonum objectum amplecti, nisi prius delectaverit: ac multo minus ad naturam voluntatis pertinet, ut si objectum bonum & jucundum ipsi offeratur, tangatur aliqua delectatione. Praesertim vero docet peccatum primum sive hominum, sive Angelorum, sine delectatione praecedenti perpetratum esse: nec ullum fuisse vel in hominibus, vel in angelis integris affectum, quo ad primum malum voluntatis actum sollicitati & invitati sint.
english: Thesis CXV. Jansenius, by contrast, does not hold that the love and desire he calls delight necessarily precede every act of the will, when the will is considered absolutely and apart from the weakness contracted through sin. This is the delight by which the will is now drawn before it freely wills and embraces anything, and by which above all it must be touched before it pursues the heavenly and spiritual good.

On his doctrine it is not simply part of the will's nature that it cannot freely embrace a good object unless the object has first delighted it. Still less does it belong to the will's nature to be touched by some delight whenever a good and pleasant object is presented to it. Above all, he teaches that the first sin, of men and of angels alike, was committed without any preceding delight, and that neither men nor angels in their unfallen state had any affection by which they were solicited and invited to the will's first evil act.
